content.text:
1) Answer

A fair proof that Keir Starmer values human rights rests on his long, consistent record across four domains: his early legal work, his policing oversight roles, his actions and statements as Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), and his explicit commitments as Prime Minister.

- Specialist human-rights lawyer and author
  - Before entering politics, Starmer specialised in human-rights litigation in the UK and overseas, including death-penalty work in the Caribbean. Encyclopaedia Britannica records his membership of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office’s death‑penalty advisory panel (2002–2008) and focus on human‑rights cases. ([britannica.com](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Keir-Starmer?utm_source=openai))
  - He wrote practitioner texts to embed the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) and the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) into UK practice, including a Cambridge University Press article guiding lawyers on the ECHR/HRA (2008) and the 1999 manual “European Human Rights Law: The Human Rights Act 1998 and the European Convention on Human Rights.” Producing tools to help courts and practitioners apply rights is evidence of valuing them. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/legal-information-management/article/european-convention-on-human-rights-and-the-human-rights-act-1998/0313F873F1E30F5C5590500416216F67?utm_source=openai))

- Independent human‑rights oversight of policing in Northern Ireland
  - From 2003–2008 he served as Human Rights Adviser to the Northern Ireland Policing Board, giving formal evidence to Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights about monitoring police compliance with human-rights standards during sensitive operations. Accepting this role, and the way he discharged it, is strong practical commitment to rights in a challenging environment. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt200506/jtselect/jtrights/uc701-iii/uc70102.htm?utm_source=openai))

- Human‑rights framing of prosecution ethics and public statements as DPP
  - As DPP, Starmer issued the CPS Statement of Ethical Principles (2 Nov 2009) foregrounding prosecutors’ duties to uphold the rule of law, fairness, openness and accountability to victims and defendants alike—explicitly rooting CPS decision‑making in human‑rights values. ([cps.gov.uk](https://www.cps.gov.uk/publication/statement-ethical-principles-public-prosecutor?utm_source=openai))
  - He also updated the Code for Crown Prosecutors (2013) to improve transparency and accessibility (including formats like Braille), consistent with equal access to justice—a rights‑based objective. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2013-01-28/debates/1301282000006/CodeForCrownProsecutors?utm_source=openai))
  - On leaving office, he publicly defended the HRA, calling repeal a “retrograde step” that would harm victims and witnesses—an unequivocal endorsement of the UK’s rights framework (14 Oct 2013). ([independent.co.uk](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/human-rights-act-must-stay-says-cps-director-keir-starmer-8877637.html))

- Explicit prime‑ministerial commitments to international human‑rights obligations
  - As Prime Minister, Starmer pledged on 4 Nov 2024 that the UK “will never withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights,” linking his approach to “profound respect for international law.” This is a clear, current commitment to maintaining the UK’s binding human‑rights obligations. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/pm-speech-to-the-interpol-general-assembly-4-november-2024?utm_source=openai))
  - The British Institute of Human Rights’ analysis of Labour’s 2024 manifesto confirms the party’s commitment to remain in the ECHR and to strengthen equality protections—policy positions set under his leadership. ([bihr.org.uk](https://www.bihr.org.uk/get-informed/legislation-explainers/uk-general-election-2024-manifestos-and-human-rights-what-do-they-say?utm_source=openai))
  - In Oct 2025 he argued for reconsidering how some ECHR provisions are interpreted in deportation cases while reaffirming that the UK will stay in the ECHR. Agreeing to remain bound by the Convention—even when proposing narrower interpretations in specific contexts—shows continuity of commitment to the overarching rights framework. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/law/2025/oct/01/keir-starmer-human-rights-law-echr-nigel-farage-small-boat-crossings?utm_source=openai))

Taken together—rights‑focused litigation and scholarship; independent human‑rights oversight of policing; embedding rights language and access principles into CPS ethics and guidance; and clear, repeated pledges to keep the UK in the ECHR—provide strong, multi‑year evidence that Keir Starmer values human rights.


2) Sources considered TRUSTWORTHY (with credibility reasoning)

- Source: GOV.UK (PM speech to the INTERPOL General Assembly: 4 November 2024)
  - Reasoning 1 (general credibility): Primary, official UK government publication; authoritative for ministers’ words and policy positions.
  - Reasoning 2 (this prompt): Direct transcript of Starmer’s own commitment that the UK will never withdraw from the ECHR; best evidence of his current stance. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/pm-speech-to-the-interpol-general-assembly-4-november-2024?utm_source=openai))

- Source: The Independent (Human Rights Act must stay, says CPS director Keir Starmer – 14 Oct 2013)
  - Reasoning 1: Established national outlet with editorial standards and fact‑checking.
  - Reasoning 2: Reports and quotes Starmer, as DPP, defending the HRA and its benefits for victims and witnesses—strong, contemporaneous evidence. ([independent.co.uk](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/human-rights-act-must-stay-says-cps-director-keir-starmer-8877637.html))

- Source: Crown Prosecution Service (Statement of Ethical Principles for the Public Prosecutor – signed 2 Nov 2009)
  - Reasoning 1: Primary institutional source for official CPS policies.
  - Reasoning 2: Contains Starmer’s own foreword setting out fairness, accountability and rule‑of‑law principles that align with human‑rights values. ([cps.gov.uk](https://www.cps.gov.uk/publication/statement-ethical-principles-public-prosecutor?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UK Parliament (Hansard/ministerial statement noting updated Code for Crown Prosecutors – 28 Jan 2013)
  - Reasoning 1: Official parliamentary record; primary source.
  - Reasoning 2: Confirms DPP‑era reforms improving transparency and accessibility—rights‑consistent objectives in prosecution policy. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2013-01-28/debates/1301282000006/CodeForCrownProsecutors?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Cambridge University Press (Keir Starmer, “The European Convention on Human Rights and the Human Rights Act 1998,” 2008)
  - Reasoning 1: Peer‑reviewed academic publisher with rigorous standards.
  - Reasoning 2: Demonstrates Starmer’s professional contribution to explaining and operationalising ECHR/HRA—evidence of valuing and disseminating human‑rights law. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/legal-information-management/article/european-convention-on-human-rights-and-the-human-rights-act-1998/0313F873F1E30F5C5590500416216F67?utm_source=openai))

- Source: AbeBooks listing (European Human Rights Law: The Human Rights Act 1998 and the ECHR, 1999)
  - Reasoning 1: Commercial bibliographic listing; useful to confirm publication details where a publisher page is not accessible.
  - Reasoning 2: Corroborates authorship of a substantial practitioner text on human‑rights law, supporting his record. ([abebooks.co.uk](https://www.abebooks.co.uk/9780905099774/European-Human-Rights-Law-Act-090509977X/plp?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UK Parliament (Joint Committee on Human Rights – evidence session with Keir Starmer QC, Human Rights Adviser to the NI Policing Board, 2006)
  - Reasoning 1: Primary, official record of select‑committee evidence.
  - Reasoning 2: Confirms his role and practical human‑rights oversight of policing—key to proving sustained commitment. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt200506/jtselect/jtrights/uc701-iii/uc70102.htm?utm_source=openai))

- Source: British Institute of Human Rights (2024 General Election: what manifestos say on human rights)
  - Reasoning 1: Specialist NGO with recognised expertise on UK human‑rights law.
  - Reasoning 2: Summarises Labour’s manifesto pledges (remain in ECHR; strengthen equality protections) set under Starmer’s leadership. ([bihr.org.uk](https://www.bihr.org.uk/get-informed/legislation-explainers/uk-general-election-2024-manifestos-and-human-rights-what-do-they-say?utm_source=openai))

- Source: The Guardian (1 Oct 2025 report on ECHR interpretation and small‑boats policy)
  - Reasoning 1: Major UK newspaper with established editorial standards.
  - Reasoning 2: Provides recent context that, while proposing narrower interpretations in specific areas, Starmer maintained the commitment to stay in the ECHR—useful nuance. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/law/2025/oct/01/keir-starmer-human-rights-law-echr-nigel-farage-small-boat-crossings?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Keir Starmer biography)
  - Reasoning 1: Reputable reference work with editorial oversight.
  - Reasoning 2: Corroborates his human‑rights litigation focus and death‑penalty advisory role, supporting the early‑career strand of the proof. ([britannica.com](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Keir-Starmer?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources considered NOT TRUSTWORTHY (and why)

- Source: GB News (examples: items asserting Starmer’s “book of woke” and pushing partisan framings)
  - Reasoning 1: TV/online outlet with a clear ideological slant; reporting often framed polemically rather than neutrally; variable sourcing.
  - Reasoning 2: For this prompt, GB News pieces did not add reliable, primary‑sourced evidence of Starmer’s human‑rights commitments beyond what neutral sources already confirm (e.g., existence of his 1999 book). I therefore did not rely on them. ([gbnews.com](https://www.gbnews.com/politics/martin-daubney-human-rights-keir-starmer-british-law?utm_source=openai))

- Source: “British Brief” (britbrief.co.uk) article alleging he “weakened” human‑rights guidance
  - Reasoning 1: Little-known site with no clear masthead or transparent editorial standards; sensational language.
  - Reasoning 2: The claims were not substantiated with primary documents and conflicted with established records from CPS and Parliament; I did not treat it as reliable. ([britbrief.co.uk](https://britbrief.co.uk/politics/liberties/starmer-edited-human-rights-manual-removing-key-protections.html?utm_source=openai))

If you want, I can also compile direct quotations from the primary sources above (e.g., the GOV.UK speech and CPS documents) alongside dates for a dossier-style brief.
